Summer flounder (Paralichthys dentatus) is a commercially important flatfish that undergoes a dramatic metamorphosis during early development, transitioning from a pelagic, bilaterally symmetrical larva to a benthic juvenile with both eyes on the left side. The early life stages begin when a fertilised ovum, measuring approximately 1.02 mm in diameter, develops into a yolk-dependent embryo. Upon eclosion at 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C], the prolarva emerges after an incubation period of just 3.06 days [ab = 3.06 days], a remarkably short duration that reflects the relatively high thermal regime typical of their estuarine nursery habitats. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, still relying on endogenous yolk reserves, has an extremely low calculated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00056 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00056 grams], a value derived from the spherical egg volume. This lecithotrophic stage persists until the mouth opens, marking the onset of exogenous feeding and the transition to an actively growing, planktonic larva.

As the pelagic larval phase progresses, individuals feed intensively on copepods and other small zooplankton, accumulating the energy reserves necessary for the profound morphological transformation that follows. Field surveys of juvenile recruits in Mid-Atlantic Bight estuaries indicate that females attain the total length at puberty at approximately 28 centimeters [Lp = approximately 28 centimeters], a size threshold that signals the onset of gametogenesis and the initiation of gonadal recrudescence. In comparison, the ultimate total length for females has been recorded at 94 centimeters [Li = 94 centimeters], indicating that these fish continue substantial somatic expansion well beyond the point of reproductive activation. This protracted growth trajectory is typical of many iteroparous flatfishes, which channel considerable resources into achieving larger body sizes that confer fecundity advantages in subsequent spawning seasons. The asymptotic size places Paralichthys dentatus among the larger-bodied members of its genus within the Paralichthyidae family, inhabiting continental shelf waters from Massachusetts to Florida.

Reproductive output in Summer flounder is closely tied to female body size, with larger individuals contributing disproportionately to population recruitment. During the autumn spawning migration to offshore continental shelf waters, gravid females produce multiple batches of pelagic eggs over the course of the spawning season. Available data indicate that fecundity per reproductive event can reach 1 to 3 million eggs per spawning batch [N_R_i = 1 to 3 million eggs per spawning batch], depending on the size and condition of the female. These fish are capable of spawning several times over the winter months, yielding approximately 8 to 12 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 8 to 12 spawning events per year], which cumulatively represents a very high annual reproductive potential. This bet-hedging strategy, in which gamete release is distributed across multiple spawning events, buffers against interannual variability in early-life survival and is a common life-history tactic among large-bodied, long-lived marine teleosts.

Adult female Summer flounder achieve a substantial ultimate wet weight of 10,600 grams [Wwi = 10,600 grams], a value that scales allometrically with the asymptotic length and reflects the considerable muscle mass and energy stores accumulated over their lifespan. This maximum recorded body mass, derived from length-weight relationships fitted to field-caught individuals, underscores the species' high somatic investment prior to and during the spawning season. At the other end of the life-history continuum, laboratory rearing studies conducted at a stable temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] have documented a maximum lifespan of approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] for individuals maintained under optimal conditions, equating to roughly 3,285 days [am = roughly 3,285 days] when expressed in calendar days. This longevity, while modest compared to some deepwater flatfishes, is sufficient to allow multiple reproductive seasons and the accumulation of significant lifetime fecundity. The relatively fast life-history pace, with early maturation and a moderate lifespan, positions the species as an r-selected strategist within the flatfish guild, capitalizing on productive temperate shelf ecosystems.

The interplay between thermal regime and physiological development is a critical determinant of early life survival in Paralichthys dentatus. Data from controlled incubation experiments demonstrate that the age at birth decreases sharply with increasing temperature, with the 3.06-day hatching time (3.06 days) [ab = 3.06 days] recorded at 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C] being considerably shorter than the hatching times observed at cooler temperatures more typical of northern estuarine nurseries in early spring. Conversely, the lifespan of 9 years [am = 9 years] recorded at 19 °C [T = 19 °C] may represent an upper thermal limit for sustained physiological function, as individuals maintained at higher temperatures often exhibit accelerated metabolic rates and reduced longevity. The 28 cm [Lp = 28 cm] total length at puberty represents a relatively early maturation relative to the 94 cm [Li = 94 cm] ultimate total length, a pattern that allows fish to contribute to the spawning stock before reaching their full growth potential. This early onset of reproduction, combined with high fecundity and a moderate lifespan, sustains the species' resilience under moderate fishing pressure, though stock assessments continue to monitor recruitment variability closely. Environmental factors such as temperature and prey availability during the early larval stages are major determinants of year-class strength, with warm springs promoting faster development and higher survival rates that ultimately influence the recruitment entering the adult population.
